title: 2026 South Carolina Gubernatorial Election
description: The 2026 South Carolina gubernatorial election will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect the next governor. Incumbent Republican Governor Henry McMaster is term-limited and cannot seek a third consecutive term. The Democratic primary held on June 9, 2026, nominated State Representative Jermaine Johnson. The Republican primary on the same date produced no majority winner, sending Lieutenant Governor Pamela Evette and Attorney General Alan Wilson to a runoff on June 23, 2026. On June 19, President Donald Trump co-endorsed both Evette and Wilson after initially endorsing only Evette, while Sen. Tim Scott, Rep. Nancy Mace, and Rep. Ralph Norman have endorsed Wilson. The Republican nominee will be heavily favored in the general election in this deep-red state, which backed Donald Trump by nearly 18 points in 2024. Democrats have not won a gubernatorial race in South Carolina since 1998.

candidates.name: Jermaine Johnson
candidates.summary: Jermaine Johnson is a member of the South Carolina House of Representatives and the Democratic nominee for governor. He has campaigned on Medicaid expansion, infrastructure investment, education reform, and addressing the state's affordability crisis. Johnson emphasizes working across the aisle and bringing a business-oriented, customer-service approach to state government.

candidates.name: Pamela Evette
candidates.summary: Pamela Evette has served as Lieutenant Governor of South Carolina since 2019 under Governor Henry McMaster. A former businesswoman, she initially received former President Donald Trump's sole endorsement in the Republican primary, but Trump later co-endorsed both Evette and her runoff opponent, Attorney General Alan Wilson, on June 19. Evette advanced to the June 23 runoff after finishing first in the June 9 primary with about 29% of the vote, and has campaigned on eliminating the state income tax, election security, and judicial reform.

candidates.name: Alan Wilson
candidates.summary: Alan Wilson has served as South Carolina's Attorney General since 2011, making him the state's longest-serving attorney general. He advanced to the June 23, 2026 Republican runoff for governor against Lieutenant Governor Pamela Evette after finishing second in the June 9 primary with about 26% of the vote. On June 19, President Donald Trump co-endorsed Wilson alongside Evette, and Sen. Tim Scott also endorsed Wilson shortly after. Wilson is a Colonel in the South Carolina Army National Guard and a combat veteran who deployed to Iraq, and has been endorsed by former Republican primary opponents Rep. Nancy Mace, Rep. Ralph Norman, and Sen. Josh Kimbrell.

Immigration.stance: Wilson advocates strong immigration enforcement: deny state benefits to illegal residents, enforce South Carolina's immigration laws, and back state and local cooperation with federal authorities to enforce immigration policy (including programs such as the 28(7)g program). He has noted he is the only candidate in the race who has defended immigration enforcement in court.

Education.stance: Alan Wilson's Education plan prioritizes fully funding public schools, expanding school choice to give families more control, improving early childhood literacy, and strengthening technical and vocational education. He also emphasizes empowering parents to participate in their children's education and to oppose what his campaign describes as woke politics in the classroom, and would expand School Resource Officer programs to keep schools safe.

He will also seek to lower property taxes for seniors and veterans and launch a comprehensive audit of state and local governments to root out waste while prioritizing small-business growth and workforce development.

Climate/Energy.stance: Wilson has opposed federal climate regulations and joined lawsuits against California and other states over climate litigation targeting energy companies. He joined a lawsuit challenging Biden's order to consider greenhouse gas costs and another challenging the revocation of the Keystone XL Pipeline permit. He has also sought to toss Charleston's climate liability lawsuit. His campaign emphasizes affordable electricity and opposing ESG mandates.

He supported the state's 2023 Fetal Heartbeat and Protection from Abortion Act and joined a 2021 Supreme Court filing calling for the overturn of Roe v. Wade. However, during the 2026 gubernatorial campaign he stated he would veto a bill eliminating abortion exceptions for rape, incest, and fatal fetal anomalies.

Firearms & Second Amendment.stance: Wilson describes himself as a fierce defender of the Second Amendment. As Attorney General, he has sued to strike down parts of the National Firearms Act, won a lawsuit against the City of Columbia over local gun laws, and defended gun manufacturers from liability lawsuits. He has received NRA endorsements in past elections.

Foreign Policy.stance: Wilson has combated Hamas-linked financing by requesting financial documents from non-profits potentially linked to Hamas support. He joined Republican attorneys general urging Congress to permanently cut ties with UN aid groups in Gaza, and joined a 25-state friend-of-the-court brief seeking to hold organizations accountable for supporting Hamas. His campaign emphasizes standing with President Trump and the America First agenda on national security issues.

Civil Rights & Equality.stance: Wilson has described himself as a defender of religious liberty and conservative values. His campaign materials state he has fought against what he calls the 'Biden transgender agenda' and he opposed same-sex marriage as Attorney General. He supports legislation protecting free speech and religious freedom, and his education platform includes opposing political agendas in classrooms.

Tech & AI.stance: Wilson has supported legislation (S.28) criminalizing the possession and distribution of AI-generated child sexual abuse material. He also joined a bipartisan coalition of attorneys general opposing a federal proposal that would bar states from enforcing AI regulations, and has called for clearer guidelines regulating AI use in political advertising to combat deepfakes and protect election integrity.

He joined 20 other states in a Supreme Court brief supporting a Pennsylvania election integrity law and has advocated for clear, consistent national election standards.

reviews.summary: This is a well-sourced, comprehensive profile of the 2026 South Carolina gubernatorial race with three candidates. Strengths include: (1) Strong sourcing across all 12 policy issues for Johnson and Wilson, with high-confidence citations from official campaign sites, government records, and credible news outlets; (2) Accurate and detailed career histories for all three candidates, with specific dates and accomplishments; (3) Neutral, consistent terminology across candidates—stances are described using each candidate's own framing (e.g., Johnson 'supports protecting women's reproductive rights' vs. Evette 'anti-abortion'), avoiding loaded language; (4) Transparent documentation of low-confidence positions (e.g., Foreign Policy for Johnson, Healthcare for Evette) with explicit notation of search attempts; (5) Balanced issue coverage across all three candidates with comparable depth. Minor gaps exist in Evette's Healthcare and Immigration positions, but these reflect genuine absence of public statements rather than research failure. Finance data is current and well-sourced. Overall, the profile demonstrates strong epistemological discipline and fairness.

forecast.rationale: No general-election polling is provided, and the only numeric poll is a Republican primary poll that does not inform the November head-to-head directly. Still, the available race data strongly favors the eventual Republican nominee: South Carolina is described as a deep-red state that backed Donald Trump by nearly 18 points in 2024, Republicans hold the governorship, and Democrats have not won a South Carolina gubernatorial race since 1998. The Democratic nominee, Jermaine Johnson, appears substantially less funded and lower-profile statewide than either major Republican contender. Because the Republican nominee is not yet determined and there is no general-election polling, confidence is medium rather than high.
